**AlertMesh**

An offline mesh communication system for disaster response

A pure-software Android application in which every phone becomes a node in a self-forming mesh network. Encrypted text, walkie-talkie voice, and triage-aware emergency alerts relay from phone to phone across multiple hops - with no internet, no cellular network, and no additional hardware of any kind.

| **Field**         | **Detail**                                                                      |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Project title     | AlertMesh - Offline Mesh Communication System for Disaster Response             |

| Interface         | CLI / terminal-themed, with a graphical emergency path                          |

# **1\. Abstract**

When a flood, earthquake, or cyclone strikes, communication is the first thing to fail. Cell towers lose power, internet backhaul is severed, and cloud services become unreachable. Survivors and rescuers can be a few hundred metres apart with no way to find each other.

AlertMesh addresses this using only devices people already carry. Two Android phones can communicate directly over Bluetooth and Wi-Fi Direct without any intervening infrastructure. AlertMesh extends this from a pair to a network: each phone relays traffic for its neighbours, so a message travels from phone to phone until it reaches its destination, connecting people who are far outside each other's direct radio range.

The engineering contribution is not the chat application but the **protocol layer** beneath it - an authenticated, delay-tolerant flooding protocol with hop-limited forwarding, duplicate suppression, replay protection and partition healing - together with a **reproducible simulation harness** that runs the real application binary across many virtual nodes, so every result can be re-verified on any laptop without a farm of test devices.

**Scope statement.** The project is entirely software. There is no custom hardware, no radio module, and no required sensor. The relative-height feature described in Section 6 is explicitly **optional** and is not on the critical path.

# **2\. Problem statement**

India experiences disruptive flooding every monsoon season. In the affected window, three failures compound:

- **Infrastructure failure.** Towers, routers and fibre are damaged or lose power. Mobile data and voice both stop.
- **Localisation failure.** Rescue teams cannot determine where survivors are, and survivors cannot signal their position.
- **Coordination failure.** Groups of survivors within walking distance of each other operate blind, unable to pool resources or share hazard information.

Existing solutions require either infrastructure that has already failed (cellular, or satellite phones at cost) or dedicated hardware that is not already in people's hands (VHF radios, LoRa devices). The gap is a system that works on unmodified consumer phones, immediately, with nothing else present.

## **2.1 What fails and what survives**

| **Fails during a disaster**               | **Survives a disaster**           |
| ----------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Cell towers (power loss, physical damage) | Bluetooth radio (phone to phone)  |
| Internet backhaul and fibre               | Wi-Fi Direct (no router required) |
| Wi-Fi routers                             | GPS satellites (solar powered)    |
| Cloud servers and messaging services      | Phone battery (6-12 hours)        |

AlertMesh depends on nothing in the left-hand column. Battery is the binding constraint, which is why power management is treated as a first-class feature rather than an afterthought.

# **3\. Solution overview**

## **3.1 The core idea**

Consider a human chain passing water buckets. No individual can reach the fire, but each person passes to the next, and the bucket arrives. AlertMesh applies this to messages.

Phone A cannot reach Phone C - they are too far apart. But Phone B sits between them. When A transmits, B receives the message, recognises that it is not the final destination, and rebroadcasts it. C receives it from B. A and C have communicated without ever being in direct range, and without either user doing anything.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

_Figure 1 - Multi-hop relay: the central mechanism of the project._

Repeat across five devices and the network spans roughly 500 to 750 metres in open ground. Each additional participant extends the reach of the whole network rather than merely joining it.

## **3.2 Why this is not trivial**

The radio API provides links between neighbours. It does **not** provide routing. Everything that makes a mesh work has to be built: deciding when to forward, preventing messages from circulating forever, proving a message really came from who it claims, recovering messages missed while disconnected, and doing all of this without draining the battery. That layer is the substance of the project.

# **4\. Project objectives**

- Design and implement an authenticated, delay-tolerant mesh protocol supporting multi-hop message delivery between Android devices with no infrastructure.
- Provide encrypted text messaging, adaptive walkie-talkie voice, and triage-aware emergency alerts over that protocol.
- Guarantee message authenticity so that emergency alerts cannot be forged or replayed by any relaying device.
- Implement store-and-forward recovery so that a device rejoining the network receives everything it missed.
- Build a reproducible, topology-controlled simulation harness that runs the real application logic without requiring multiple physical devices.
- Measure the protocol quantitatively - delivery ratio, hop latency, rebroadcast efficiency and recovery time - and report the results with their method stated.
- Deliver the whole system as software only, with no custom hardware and no required sensors.

# **5\. Core features and how they work**

Nine required features. Every one is achievable in software, testable without additional devices, and demonstrable on a laptop.

## **5.1 Automatic device discovery**

**What it does.** Opening the app makes the device visible to, and aware of, every nearby phone running AlertMesh. There is no pairing, no password and no user action.

**How it works.** Each device simultaneously advertises its presence and scans for advertisements using the Google Nearby Connections API, which multiplexes Bluetooth LE for discovery and Wi-Fi Direct for bulk transfer and handles vendor differences internally. When two devices detect each other they perform an automatic connection handshake, exchange public keys and derive a shared link key. A short randomised back-off before accepting connections prevents the churn that occurs when both sides attempt to initiate simultaneously.

## **5.2 Multi-hop mesh relay**

**What it does.** Messages travel across intermediate phones to reach recipients outside direct radio range. This is the central mechanism of the project.

**How it works.** Every message is wrapped in an envelope:

msgId 16-byte ULID, time-sortable and globally unique

origin sender device identifier

counter monotonic per-sender sequence number

type TEXT | VOICE | SOS | PRESENCE | SYNC_REQ | SYNC_RESP

channel walkie-talkie channel, 0-8

ttl hop budget, default 8 - MUTABLE

payload AES-256-GCM encrypted content

sig Ed25519 signature over all fields EXCEPT ttl

On receiving a frame, a node runs an ordered pipeline. Cheap checks come first, so that an attacker cannot exhaust the CPU by flooding invalid signatures:

- **Duplicate check.** If the message ID is in the seen-cache, discard. This is what prevents messages circulating forever.
- **Replay check.** If the sequence number is at or below the high-water mark recorded for that sender, discard.
- **Rate limit.** A token bucket per neighbour caps the inbound message rate.
- **Signature verification.** Only now is the expensive elliptic-curve check performed.
- **Local delivery**, then decrement TTL. If TTL reaches zero, stop.
- **Jittered rebroadcast.** Wait 50-250 ms at random, then forward to all neighbours except the one it arrived from.

Two refinements make this efficient rather than merely correct. **Split horizon** never returns a message to its sender. **Counter-based suppression** cancels the rebroadcast if two or more neighbours have already been heard rebroadcasting the same message - those neighbours have already covered the area, so transmitting again wastes battery and airtime without improving delivery.

**Implementation warning.** The TTL field changes at every hop. If it is included in the signed bytes, every signature check fails after the first hop, and the failure is silent. Exclude it explicitly from both signing and verification.

## **5.3 Encrypted text messaging**

**What it does.** Text messages that only the intended recipients can read, and which cannot be forged or altered by any relaying device.

**How it works.** On first launch each device generates an Ed25519 identity keypair stored in the Android Keystore. The device identifier is derived from the public key and displayed as a four-word fingerprint, such as tiger-north-42-blue, so two users can verify each other by reading it aloud.

| **Traffic type** | **Protection**                                                           |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Neighbour link   | X25519 ECDH, HKDF-derived AES-256-GCM link key                           |
| Mesh broadcast   | Shared session key, distributed over the already-encrypted link          |
| Direct message   | ECIES to the recipient's public key - relays carry it but cannot read it |
| All messages     | Ed25519 signature by the originator                                      |

When two previously separate meshes meet, the session key belonging to the numerically lower device identifier wins and the other side re-keys. The rule is deterministic, so the merge cannot deadlock.

**Trust model, stated honestly.** No certificate authority can be reached offline, so this is trust-on-first-use with visible fingerprints - the same model as Signal's safety numbers. It does not prevent an attacker generating many false identities. That limitation is documented rather than concealed.

## **5.4 Walkie-talkie voice**

**What it does.** Press and hold to speak, release to stop, exactly like a handheld radio. Channels 1 to 8 allow separate groups to operate without interfering.

**How it works - adaptive transmission.** Live audio degrades badly over multiple hops, because each relay adds latency and jitter. Rather than either forcing live audio everywhere or abandoning it, the app selects the mode automatically based on the recipient's hop count:

| **Distance** | **Mode** | **Mechanism**                                | **Indicator** |
| ------------ | -------- | -------------------------------------------- | ------------- |
| 1 hop        | Live     | Continuous stream payload, 50-150 ms latency | Green LIVE    |
| 2+ hops      | Relayed  | Record fully, then flood as a voice note     | Amber RELAYED |

The user never chooses. The app degrades gracefully and states which mode is active, so the person speaking knows whether they are being heard immediately or after a delay.

**Audio pipeline.** Capture at 8 kHz mono through AudioRecord; encode to AMR-NB at 12.2 kbit/s using MediaCodec, an encoder guaranteed present on every Android device; frame at 20 ms; buffer 200 ms on the receiving side to absorb jitter; play through AudioTrack in streaming mode. A ten-second transmission is roughly 15 KB.

**Encrypting a stream efficiently.** Signing every 20 ms frame would mean fifty elliptic-curve operations per second and would exhaust the battery. Instead the sender signs a single stream header at session start, which the receiver verifies once to authenticate the entire stream. Individual frames are then protected with AES-256-GCM using a nonce built from the stream identifier and a frame counter, giving confidentiality, integrity and replay protection at negligible cost.

## **5.5 SOS with triage**

**What it does.** A single action broadcasts an emergency alert to every device in the mesh. Receiving phones display a full-screen alarm.

**How it works.** The alert carries structured information that responders actually need, rather than only a location:

peopleCount how many people are present

injuredCount how many are injured

condition TRAPPED | INJURED | SAFE | NEED_WATER | NEED_MEDICAL

note free text, 100 characters maximum

location latitude, longitude, accuracy radius, fix age

The alert floods the mesh with a raised TTL and elevated priority, pre-empting any active voice channel. Because every message is signed, an alert that fails verification is discarded silently and never displayed - a false emergency cannot be injected by anyone lacking the sender's private key.

**Location honesty.** Assisted GPS data normally arrives over the network. Without connectivity, a cold satellite fix can take minutes. The app therefore maintains a warm fix, refreshing position periodically while the app is active, and every alert carries both the accuracy radius and the age of the fix. The receiving screen shows these plainly, for example "±30 m, fix 4 minutes old". If no fix is available the alert is still sent, flagged as having no current position. A stale coordinate is never presented as if it were live.

For future integration with official agencies, the relevant standard is the Common Alerting Protocol (CAP), the format used internationally for emergency alert interchange.

## **5.6 Store-and-forward and partition healing**

**What it does.** A phone that moves out of range and later returns receives everything it missed. Messages sent to an unreachable person are delivered when they reconnect.

**How it works.** Each node maintains a digest - a map of every sender it has heard from to the highest sequence number seen from that sender. When a new connection is established, both sides exchange digests, compute what the other lacks and request the missing ranges. Recovery is bounded to the last 24 hours or 500 messages to prevent an unbounded transfer. Store-and-forward is therefore not a separate feature but a natural consequence of the synchronisation mechanism.

## **5.7 Presence and network awareness**

**What it does.** Every participant can see who is in the network, how far away in hops, how much battery they have left, and how recently they were heard.

**How it works.** Each node floods a compact signed presence beacon every 10 seconds, extending to 30 seconds in power-saving mode. The beacon carries battery percentage, hop count (incremented by each relay), GPS position and accuracy where available, and sensor availability flags. At roughly 60 bytes across ten nodes this costs about 60 bytes per second - negligible. The hop count carried in the beacon is what drives the automatic live-versus-relayed decision for voice.

## **5.8 Distance estimation**

**What it does.** Shows how far away another participant is.

**How it works - hybrid.** When both devices have a recent GPS fix of adequate accuracy, distance is computed directly using the haversine formula and reported with a confidence figure. Indoors, where GPS is unreliable or absent, the app falls back to estimating from received signal strength using a log-distance path-loss model. Radio signal strength is heavily distorted by multipath reflection, so this fallback is presented as a band - "very close", "nearby", "some distance", "far" - rather than a spurious precise figure. Signal samples are smoothed with a median filter rather than a mean, because multipath produces spikes that destroy an average.

## **5.9 Power management**

**What it does.** Extends operating time when charging is unavailable, and warns when other participants are close to failing.

**How it works.** Measurement drives the design here rather than assumption. Radio scanning consumes on the order of 10 to 30 milliwatts; the display consumes 500 to 800. The dominant saving therefore comes from operating with the screen off, using haptic and audible alerts and waking the display only for emergencies. Below a configurable threshold the app additionally lengthens the discovery duty cycle and the presence beacon interval. Every participant's battery level is visible to the others, so a group can see which nodes - and therefore which relay paths - are about to disappear.

**A platform obstacle that must be solved early.** Several manufacturers common in India aggressively terminate background applications, which would silently kill the mesh whenever the screen locks. The countermeasures are a foreground service declared with the connected-device type, a persistent notification, a battery-optimisation exemption prompt at first run, and manufacturer-specific auto-start guidance. This must be verified in Stage 2 rather than discovered in Stage 5.

# **6\. Optional feature - relative height**

**This feature is optional.** It requires a barometric pressure sensor, which many budget phones do not include. It is implemented behind an interface that returns no value when unsupported, so its absence changes nothing elsewhere in the system. It is scheduled for the final stage and is not on the critical path.

## **6.1 What it would do**

Report not only how far away another person is, but how far above or below - for example, "45 m away, 18 m above you, approximately 6 floors up". In a multi-storey building this is the difference between knowing someone is nearby and knowing where to go.

## **6.2 Why the obvious approaches fail**

| **Approach**          | **Assessment**                                                         |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| GPS altitude          | Vertical error of 15-30 m, equivalent to roughly nine floors. Unusable |
| Wi-Fi round-trip time | Accurate to 1-2 m but supported only on flagship hardware              |
| Signal strength       | Cannot distinguish vertical from horizontal separation                 |
| Barometric difference | Approximately 1 m when calibrated. This is the viable method           |

## **6.3 The mechanism**

Atmospheric pressure decreases predictably with altitude. A phone's barometer reports absolute pressure, which drifts substantially with weather - but both phones sit within the same weather system, so that error is common to both readings and cancels when the two are subtracted. The system does not measure altitude; it measures the difference, which is far more reliable.

Hypsometric relation:

delta_h = 8435 \* ln( P_you / P_them ) metres

where 8435 m is the atmospheric scale height at 288 K.

Near sea level this gives approximately 1 hPa per 8.4 m,

so six storeys (about 19 m) appear as a 2.3 hPa difference -

comfortably larger than sensor noise.

## **6.4 The calibration problem**

Every barometer has a fixed manufacturing offset of roughly ±1 hPa, which corresponds to a constant error of about ±8 m, or two to three floors, between any two devices. Comparing raw readings therefore produces confidently wrong floor numbers.

The remedy is a one-time handshake: when two users are physically on the same level, either taps "we are on the same level" and the app records and permanently stores the pressure offset for that pairing. Accuracy afterwards is approximately ±1 m. Where no calibration exists, the interface shows a direction and a range only, and **never a floor number** - being vague and correct is preferable to being precise and wrong. A rapid rate of pressure change indicates the user is in a lift, in which case the reading is frozen and labelled accordingly.

## **6.5 Validation without extra devices**

The arithmetic for "phone A versus phone B" is identical to that for "one phone at two moments" - a pressure difference either way. The feature can therefore be validated with a single device by walking from the ground floor to the sixth, logging pressure continuously and comparing computed height against tape-measured floor heights. The Android emulator also exposes a simulated pressure sensor, so the entire pipeline can be unit-tested with no physical sensor at all.

# **7\. System architecture**

## **7.1 Layered design**

![](data:image/png;base64,)

_Figure 2 - Four-layer architecture. Only the bottom layer knows what carries the bytes._

## **7.2 The transport abstraction**

Everything above the bottom layer is written against a single interface:

interface MeshTransport {

val localId: DeviceId

val peers: StateFlow&lt;Set<DeviceId&gt;>

val inbound: Flow&lt;InboundFrame&gt;

suspend fun start()

suspend fun stop()

suspend fun send(to: DeviceId, bytes: ByteArray): Result&lt;Unit&gt;

suspend fun broadcast(bytes: ByteArray)

}

This single decision is what makes the project buildable by one developer with one phone. The routing, cryptography, persistence and synchronisation logic - the great majority of the work and all of its difficulty - can be developed and tested entirely on a laptop, because the radio can be substituted for something that behaves like a radio.

## **7.3 The three transports**

| **Transport**     | **Purpose**                                      | **Runs on**                    |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------ |
| LoopbackTransport | Unit tests: routing, dedup, TTL, crypto, sync    | Laptop, JUnit                  |
| SocketTransport   | Full application across several nodes - the demo | 3 emulators + 1 phone          |
| NearbyTransport   | Real radio validation (optional)                 | Physical devices, if available |

## **7.4 The rendezvous server**

A small laptop process that relays frames **only between nodes declared adjacent**. If nodes A and C are not neighbours in the configured topology, no frame can pass directly between them regardless of what the application attempts. Multi-hop is therefore genuinely enforced rather than simulated, and the router must really work for messages to arrive.

The server supports live control during a demonstration: reconfiguring the topology between line, ring and star; partitioning the network into isolated groups and healing it; and injecting packet loss at a chosen rate.

**This turns the constraint into a capability.** A network can be partitioned and healed on command, and packet loss dialled to 30 per cent, live on screen. Three physical phones cannot demonstrate either reliably - a radio link cannot be severed on stage on cue.

# **8\. Technology stack**

## **8.1 Core technologies**

| **Concern**          | **Technology**                        | **Rationale**                                                      |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Language             | Kotlin                                | First-class Android language; coroutines suit an event-driven mesh |
| IDE                  | Android Studio                        | Standard toolchain, emulator management                            |
| Minimum SDK          | API 24 (Android 7.0)                  | Broad device coverage                                              |
| Target SDK           | API 35                                | Current permission model                                           |
| Architecture         | MVVM with StateFlow                   | Reactive state fits streaming mesh events                          |
| UI toolkit           | Jetpack Compose                       | Declarative; full control for a custom terminal renderer           |
| Radio layer          | Google Nearby Connections             | Abstracts Bluetooth and Wi-Fi Direct across vendors                |
| Cryptography         | Google Tink                           | Audited primitives; avoids hand-rolled crypto                      |
| Serialisation        | kotlinx-serialization (protobuf)      | Compact wire format, versionable, no manual byte handling          |
| Persistence          | Room (SQLite)                         | Messages, peers, dedup cache, metrics                              |
| Location             | FusedLocationProvider                 | Satellite fix without network assistance                           |
| Audio                | AudioRecord / AudioTrack / MediaCodec | AMR-NB encoder guaranteed on all devices                           |
| Concurrency          | Kotlin Coroutines and Flow            | Structured concurrency for many parallel links                     |
| Testing              | JUnit with a virtual-node harness     | Multi-node behaviour tested without devices                        |
| Dependency injection | Manual container (no Hilt)            | Annotation-processing overhead not justified for a solo build      |

## **8.2 Cryptographic primitives**

| **Purpose**                 | **Primitive**      | **Tink API**                    |
| --------------------------- | ------------------ | ------------------------------- |
| Device identity and signing | Ed25519            | PublicKeySign / PublicKeyVerify |
| Link key agreement          | X25519 ECDH + HKDF | Hybrid key template             |
| Direct message encryption   | ECIES              | HybridEncrypt / HybridDecrypt   |
| Payload and voice frames    | AES-256-GCM        | Aead                            |
| Key storage                 | Android Keystore   | AndroidKeysetManager            |

## **8.3 Terminal interface stack**

| **Concern** | **Choice**                             | **Rationale**                                            |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| Rendering   | LazyColumn of AnnotatedString          | Native performance, per-character colour control         |
| Typeface    | JetBrains Mono (OFL)                   | Designed for terminals; free to redistribute             |
| Input       | BasicTextField, not TextField          | Material styling would have to be fought, not configured |
| Parser      | Hand-written token dispatch            | About 150 lines; no dependency risk                      |
| History     | DataStore, last 100 commands           | Recall via arrow keys                                    |
| Completion  | Prefix trie over commands and peer IDs | Tab completion                                           |

**Two settings decide whether the terminal is usable.** Autocorrect must be disabled on the input field, or the keyboard will capitalise commands and rewrite peer identifiers. And because Android soft keyboards provide no Tab, arrow or slash keys, a scrollable key row must be pinned above the keyboard.

## **8.4 Considered and rejected**

| **Alternative**               | **Reason for rejection**                                                                                                   |
| ----------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Raw Wi-Fi Direct API          | Behaves inconsistently across manufacturers; Nearby handles this internally                                                |
| WebView with xterm.js         | Real ANSI emulation, but inserts a JavaScript bridge between the Kotlin mesh core and the display for a purely visual gain |
| Custom cryptography           | No justification for hand-rolling primitives that Tink provides audited                                                    |
| LoRa radio module             | Would extend range to kilometres but introduces a hardware dependency. Documented as future scope                          |
| Live voice over multiple hops | Latency and jitter across relays make speech unintelligible; replaced by adaptive relayed voice notes                      |

# **9\. Interface theme - terminal UI**

## **9.1 Rationale**

The interface is styled as a command-line terminal. This is not only an aesthetic choice. The project's substance is a network protocol, and a terminal is the native interface for network tools - ping, traceroute and route inspection all work this way. Commands map one-to-one onto real protocol operations, and the scrollback is the mesh event log.

It also solves a presentation problem. A conventional chat interface conceals precisely what the project is about: hop counts, signature verification, suppression behaviour and partition recovery. A terminal displays them. Every message line carries its own routing metadata, so an observer sees the protocol working rather than being asked to take it on trust.

## **9.2 Boot sequence**

AlertMesh v0.1.0-rc1 . build 2026.07.30

\[ OK \] Keystore unlocked

\[ OK \] Identity: tiger-north-42-blue

\[ OK \] Transport: socket (rendezvous 10.0.2.2:9999)

\[ OK \] Router online ttl=8 dedup=5000 suppress=2

\[ OK \] Store: 1,284 messages . 6 peers known

\[ WARN \] Barometer absent - height reporting disabled

\[ WARN \] Location services OFF - run /fix

\[ OK \] Listening.

type /help for commands

mesh://tiger-north-42 \$

The warning lines double as the permission and readiness check, replacing a separate preflight screen.

## **9.3 Command set**

| **Command**                    | **Function**                                                             |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| /scan                          | Begin discovery, streaming peers as they appear                          |
| /peers                         | Table of participants: hops, battery, distance, height, signature status |
| /net                           | Live topology rendered as an ASCII graph                                 |
| /trace &lt;peer&gt;            | Route path with per-hop latency and signal strength                      |
| /stat                          | Routing, cryptographic and power counters                                |
| /msg &lt;peer&gt; &lt;text&gt; | Direct message, readable only by the recipient                           |
| /all &lt;text&gt;              | Broadcast to the mesh                                                    |
| /ptt &lt;peer&gt;              | Push-to-talk; live at one hop, relayed beyond                            |
| /ch &lt;1-8&gt;                | Select walkie-talkie channel                                             |
| /sos                           | Open the graphical triage form                                           |
| /safe                          | Broadcast that you are unharmed; cancels your alert                      |
| /key \[peer\]                  | Show fingerprint for out-of-band verification                            |
| /log \[level\]                 | Live event stream at chosen verbosity                                    |
| /sim ...                       | Development only: partition, heal, packet loss, topology                 |

## **9.4 The trace command**

Standard traceroute relies on TTL expiry combined with reverse routing, which a flooding mesh does not provide. Route recording is used instead: an optional field in the envelope to which each relay appends its own identifier before forwarding, with the destination echoing the accumulated path back to the sender. The cost is one field and three lines in the router.

mesh://tiger-north-42 \$ /trace priya-s

0 tiger-north-42-blue (you) 0 ms

1 amber-west-11-red rssi -61 -> 84 ms

2 quiet-east-07-grey rssi -73 -> 201 ms

3 priya-s rssi -68 -> 288 ms

3 hops . 288 ms . sig ok . 412 bytes

No other single output demonstrates multi-hop relay as clearly.

## **9.5 Dual-mode interface**

A command line is unsuitable for a distressed, injured or non-English-speaking user. Rather than compromise the terminal, the interface operates in two modes serving two distinct users.

- **Operator mode** - the terminal. For a coordinator or volunteer with time and training. Full protocol visibility.
- **Emergency mode** - always reachable, never typed. A persistent alert control remains pinned at the base of the screen and never scrolls away. The alert form is graphical, not typed. An incoming alert seizes the entire display at maximum brightness with an audible alarm, large text, icons and regional language support, replacing the terminal until dismissed.

Stated as a design position: a dual-mode interface serving a trained operator who benefits from protocol visibility and a distressed survivor who needs a single large target, with emergency paths bypassing the command line entirely.

# **10\. Development and validation approach**

## **10.1 Constraint**

Development uses one Android phone and a laptop. No additional devices are purchased or borrowed. This constraint shapes the architecture rather than limiting the outcome.

## **10.2 Running a multi-node network on one laptop**

Three Android Virtual Devices are created in Android Studio and launched together, each connecting to the rendezvous server. Practical notes:

- Emulators reach the host laptop at address **10.0.2.2** - this is the rendezvous server's address from inside an emulator.
- **Mock GPS** coordinates can be assigned to each emulator individually through Extended Controls, so the distance feature functions fully.
- The **host microphone** can be routed to the virtual device, so walkie-talkie transmission is demonstrable.
- A **simulated pressure sensor** is available for the optional height module.
- If the laptop cannot host three emulators, the mesh core is plain Kotlin and can run as headless console nodes - itself a demonstration that the protocol implementation is platform-independent.

## **10.3 What is claimed, and what is not**

The project claims a correctly implemented and reproducibly validated protocol. It does not claim field-measured radio performance. Results are reported with their method attached, and the limitations section states plainly which measurements are simulated and which are real. Precision about method is what separates a simulation from a fabrication.

# **11\. Project stages**

The work is organised into five stages across ten weeks. Each stage has a defined deliverable and an exit criterion that must be met before moving on.

## **11.2 Week-by-week plan**

| **Week** | **Deliverable**                                                                              | **Exit criterion**                                            |
| -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1        | Transport interface, loopback transport, virtual-node harness, project skeleton              | Six virtual nodes exchange frames in a unit test              |
| 2        | Envelope (protobuf), router: TTL, dedup, split horizon, suppression, metrics                 | Five-hop delivery; loop test and 20% packet-loss test pass    |
| 3        | Cryptography: Ed25519 identity, X25519, session keys, ordered receive pipeline, rate limiter | Tampered, replayed and flooded messages are all rejected      |
| 4        | Rendezvous server, socket transport, foreground service, background survival                 | Three emulators form a line; A reaches C through B            |
| 5        | Terminal UI, command parser, chat, Room persistence, presence beacon                         | Peer table shows hops, battery and signature status           |
| 6        | Partition healing and digest synchronisation                                                 | A node offline for five minutes recovers everything it missed |
| 7        | Walkie-talkie: live one-hop, relayed multi-hop, channels, busy indication                    | Automatic fallback verified at two hops                       |
| 8        | SOS with triage, emergency mode, GPS distance, regional language                             | Forged alert dropped; distance correct with mocked GPS        |
| 9        | Measurement runs and suppression ablation study                                              | Six metrics collected across three topologies                 |
| 10       | Optional height module, report, demo rehearsal, repository upload                            | Demonstration runs ten times without failure                  |

## **11.3 Gates and contingency**

**Week 4 and Week 6 are the two hard gates.** Week 4 proves that a real multi-node network runs; Week 6 proves that the network recovers from partition. If either slips, features are cut rather than deadlines moved.

**Cut order if time runs short:** the optional height module first, then the walkie-talkie channel system, then regional language strings. The evaluation in Stage 5 is never cut - a working protocol with measured results is worth more than additional features with none.

**Weeks 1 to 3 require no phone at all**, so development can begin immediately and the highest-risk logic is finished before any device dependency appears.

# **12\. Evaluation and results**

A demonstration shows that something runs. Measurements show how well. Six results, each labelled with its method.

| **#** | **Metric**                                                        | **Method**                            |
| ----- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| 1     | Delivery ratio against hop count, 1 to 5                          | Simulated, line topology              |
| 2     | End-to-end latency added per hop                                  | Simulated, declared per-link latency  |
| 3     | Redundant rebroadcast ratio, suppression on versus off            | Simulated ablation - principal result |
| 4     | Delivery under 0, 10, 20 and 30 per cent packet loss              | Simulated                             |
| 5     | Partition recovery time and completeness                          | Simulated                             |
| 6     | Cryptographic throughput: verifications and signatures per second | Measured on physical hardware         |

Result 3 is the principal contribution: a controlled comparison showing how much redundant transmission the suppression mechanism eliminates, and at what cost to delivery ratio. Result 6 is real hardware data obtained from a single device.

If a barometer is available, a seventh result is added: reported against actual floor separation, calibrated and uncalibrated, obtained by walking a stairwell with one phone.

# **13\. Demonstration plan**

Three emulator windows and the rendezvous console, projected together.

- **Topology.** Configure a line. Nodes A and C are not connected to each other.
- **Relay.** Type on A; it appears on C. The console log shows B forwarding it - an actual relay, not a depiction of one.
- **Loop prevention.** Reconfigure as a ring and send a message. The duplicate counter demonstrates that it did not circulate indefinitely.
- **Trace.** Run /trace and display the full hop path with per-hop timing.
- **Partition.** Isolate a node and send three messages. Nothing arrives. Heal the network; all three are delivered at once.
- **Walkie-talkie.** Transmit to a neighbour - live. Transmit to a distant node - the indicator switches to relayed automatically.
- **Emergency.** Submit a triage alert; every node alarms. Inject a forged alert from the console; it is discarded silently.
- **Degradation.** Raise packet loss to 30 per cent and watch delivery ratio fall in real time.
- **Results.** Display the suppression ablation chart.

Steps 5 and 8 cannot be performed reliably with physical phones, because a radio link cannot be severed on command. The development constraint produces a stronger demonstration than the unconstrained version would have.

# **14\. Limitations**

- **The radio layer is not validated on hardware.** The Nearby Connections transport is implemented against the same interface but has not been field-tested. Reported results derive from the socket transport with declared latency and loss parameters.
- **Results are simulated except where stated.** Metric 6 is measured on a physical device; metrics 1 to 5 are simulated with parameters given.
- **Range is not measured.** Published figures for the underlying transport are cited rather than independently reproduced.
- **Trust is established on first use.** No offline certificate authority exists, so an attacker able to generate many identities is not prevented from doing so.
- **Flooding does not scale beyond tens of nodes.** Distance-vector or link-state routing would be required for hundreds; this is future work.
- **Relays observe metadata.** Message content is protected, but the communication graph - who contacts whom, and how often - is visible to intermediate nodes.
- **Height detection is optional and unvalidated at scale.** Implemented and unit-tested against simulated pressure; validated on a single device at most.
- **Battery bounds everything.** Six to twelve hours of phone battery caps the usable window regardless of protocol efficiency.
- **The application must already be installed.** Distribution before or during an event is an unsolved adoption problem, not a technical one.

# **15\. Future scope**

- **LoRa radio over USB.** A module costing roughly ₹1,600 per node would extend each hop from under 200 metres to between 2 and 10 kilometres, changing the system from building-scale to district-scale.
- **CAP integration.** Consuming official alerts in Common Alerting Protocol format through any node retaining connectivity, and flooding them to the rest of the mesh.
- **Scalable routing.** Replacing controlled flooding with AODV or OLSR-class routing for networks of hundreds of nodes.
- **Bluetooth GATT transport.** A second transport implementation removing the Google Play Services dependency. The transport abstraction means this requires no change above the bottom layer.
- **Field validation.** Measured range, delivery and battery figures across a genuine multi-device deployment.
- **Wi-Fi round-trip-time ranging.** Where hardware supports it, replacing signal-strength estimation with 1-2 metre distance accuracy.

# **16\. Summary**

AlertMesh is an offline, delay-tolerant mesh messaging system for Android in which every phone acts as a relay, carrying signed and encrypted text, adaptive walkie-talkie voice and triage-aware emergency alerts across multiple hops with no infrastructure of any kind. It is presented through a terminal-style interface in which each command corresponds to a real protocol operation, with a graphical emergency path that bypasses the command line for users in distress.

It is built against a transport abstraction that allows the entire network to run as a reproducible, topology-controlled simulation, so every result can be re-verified on any laptop without a device farm. It requires no custom hardware, no additional phones and no particular sensor. The relative-height capability is implemented as an optional module and is not required for the system to be complete.

**Every deliverable is code.**
